I can understand flight simulators, especially for training purposes, but I feel that these truck ones are a different breed. What is enjoyable about driving a truck around on a freeway for a half hour? If that's the simulator you're doing, why not just go be an actual truck driver? I don't think I would find the farming simulators really any more enjoyable, but I can see a slightly larger appeal to farming than driving a truck. Please help. I'm so confused :(

I'd love to hear from people who do enjoy these games.
Will someone explain the appeal of the Truck Simulator games?

It's progression mostly, and precision. It's not a racing game, but you still go for the best time within the rules of the road. Management is also meticulous and detail oriented. What you're shipping, where it's going, handling the machine properly, knowing the rules of the road, actually making the journey yourself, etc.

I got Euro Trucker 2 because it was a very early game that supported VR. The Oculus added a lot to the game, but the other elements were also a factor. It's not strenuous, though it's also not too laid back because you're dealing with a lot of aspects of the business outside of driving as well as hauling loads, delivering them, and putting what you gain back into the business while still trying to make a profit in the process.

Honestly, Elite Dangerous is somewhat similar in a lot of ways. Yes there are lasers and space ships, but it's also a lot of the same kind of resource management and hauling loads from one place to another. Even if you're playing as a space pirate, you've got to sell what you're pirating and manage fuel and resources to keep yourself in business.

Truck Simulators are really that kind of gameplay without the space and laser parts. It's more involved than region management simulators like SimCity, but not as intense as something more visceral where you're dealing with fast paced gameplay dodging bullets or hacking stuff up with a sword.

Also, as you mentioned, training. They can be good for that to a limited extent. It won't replace real world experience, but can be used to prepare for that kind of training and form good habits. Sim games tend to be designed so you follow real world rules and procedures, so they can be good teaching tools for a job, or just teach someone about an industry they're interested in even if they aren't really looking for a real world job in that field. It's a chance to try something out and see what it's like a little without actually really having to do it.

I enjoy the relaxing progression of the game. Unlike most simulator games the Truck Sim games have a progression to it and a fail state. You start out with a crappy truck and make money while managing your expenses and tiredness until you have the money to buy more and better trucks and hire NPCs to drive those trucks and add to your capitol. Driving around is fun while doing it too and trying to get to the delivery site as fast as possible without losing money for speeding. It is actually a challenge but one at a slower pace so I don't get too stressed.

Everyone has already said relaxing. I'll add one other: I work 12 hour days. On weekends, it's all about chores and family stuff I can't do during the week. I never have time to go anywhere or see anything. In the winter, I go to work when the sun isn't up yet, and go home after its gone down.

My point is, during my 1 or 2 hours a night of free time, being able to drive a truck over long haul, with beautiful graphics that mimic a drive through countryside's, makes me feel a little more grounded, and less like a wage slave

I owned an old bootleg copy of "18 Wheels of Steel" which was basically a very early version of truck simulator. Thought it was great at the time. Deliver containers across the country and get money to buy new trucks. The world map was huge, and making a mistake like jack-knifing the trailer was always a possibility.

If anything this game taught me how truck physics work. How wide to take turns, how to maneuver a multiple axeled vehicle on hinges.

The appeal would be the peaceful simplicity. Driving on the highway in the rain, winshield wipers on and soft country music on the truck radio yields a sense of peace very few games try to emulate. Most games now are so full of bells and whistles there is no place for the solitary and quiet violin.
